Virtual field optimization method (VFOM)
A B S T R A C T
Acoustic emission (AE) event location plays an important role in structural safety assessments.
However, accurately locating an AE event is usually difficult, especially for a small structure.
Interestingly, a pencil-lead break (PLB) experiment shows that the P-wave arrival time of a sensor
is always significantly different (~260 µs) from that of the other sensors. This time difference is
much greater than the P-wave travel time in the range of the experimental sample. Therefore, it
can be inferred that there is a P-wave arrival time system error (PATSE) for each sensor. The
PATSE may be due to a combined result of the sensor site effect and signal transfer delay time
from the sensor to the signal storage. To handle this, a Bayesian inversion framework was built to
estimate PATSEs. A synthetic test demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed Bayesian
method for noisy P-wave arrival time data. Then, Bayesian inversion was applied to 15 PLB
events, which confirmed the existence of PATSE in an AE experiment for the first time. The
average PATSE reached 1.47 µs without considering the P-wave arrival time significantly
different sensor. The average location error of 25 PLB events was 14.30 mm and 6.58 mm for
PATSE unremoved and removed data, respectively. To achieve this, a high-precision virtual field
optimization location method (VFOM) was used. This demonstrates the necessity of removing the
PATSEs. Finally, the AE event location performance for the PATSE unremoved and removed data
was compared, where the AE events were obtained from the uniaxial compression of a red
sandstone sample. The results indicated that there was a higher location detection success rate for
the corrected data. The AE locations based on the corrected data were in a better correlation with
the rock sample failure mode than that without correction. Moreover, increase the signal sam-
pling frequency for AE event identification, use a real-time inverted 3D velocity model and update
the PATSEs in real time could be used to further improve the AE event location accuracy.

1 Introduction
Acoustic emission (AE) monitoring takes advantage of the transient elastic wavefield generated by rapid released energy of the
material. Then, the recorded AE signals are then used for further monitoring investigations, such as waveform analysis, AE event
location, magnitude calculation, focal mechanism inversion and velocity tomography. AE waveform analysis and event location are
two effective ways to study material crack growth. For the AE waveform analysis, Bhuiyan has made a great contribution [1–5]. Their
results show a new avenue of using the piezoelectric wafer active sensors (PWAS) transducer, by capturing more frequency information
contained in the AE waveform than conventional AE sensors. Moreover, the waveform evolution is highly related to the physica
boundary conditions of the cracks, as well as the fatigue crack growth mechanism. This study focused on the AE event location, which
can provide good guidance for monitoring structural health and analysing material fracture processes [6]. However, for conventiona
location methods, the AE location result distribution may be negatively correlated with the material failure mode [7]. Currently, an AE
event location is usually performed based on P-wave travel time and ray tracing-based location methods. These location results are
largely dependent on the quality of the P-wave arrival time data and location techniques.

1.1 P-wave arrival time determination
The automatic picking of the absolute P-wave arrival time has been widely studied owing to its convenience. Allen [8] proposed the
short-term average to long-term average (STA/LTA) method, which considers the instantaneous characteristics of the first P-wave
arrival amplitude and frequency content. Sleeman and van Eck [9] assumed that the signals before and after the P-wave arrival time
have different statuses. Based on the maximum likelihood derivation, they proposed the autoregressive Akaike information criterion
(AR-AIC) picking method. In addition, the Kurtosis method, fractal dimension method and predominant period method have also been
proposed for absolute P-wave arrival time picking. These methods take advantage of the take-off amplitude of a single waveform.
However, background noise and signal propagation attenuation can affect the take-off amplitude [10].
To handle the above problem, researchers began to determine the P-wave relative delay time by performing cross-correlation on
two windowed characteristic waveforms. The cross-correlation method is mainly dependent on the main peaks of the windowed
waveforms. Compared with the absolute P-wave arrival time picking methods, cross-correlation picking is less affected by background
noise and signal attenuation. Studies have shown the effectiveness of the waveform cross-correlation method in determining the
relative delay times of earthquake waveforms [11,12] and microseismic signals [13]
The above P-wave arrival time picking methods treat the time difference between the observed waveforms as the trigger time
difference. These picking methods either set the delay time from sensor to signal storage to the same value or neglect this relative delay
time difference. However, it can be different because of the following factors: First, the sensor response time can be influenced by the
sensor checking level and sensor contacting state with the material [14]. Then, the sensor monitored signal is transmitted to an
amplifier, AE data pre-processing and storage equipment. In addition, the system synchronisation time may exhibit a different shift.
The delay time difference from sensor to signal storage is marked as the P-wave arrival time system error (PATSE). To the best of our
knowledge, PATSE has yet to be examined or estimated in an AE event location study.
1.2 AE event location methods
For the ray tracing-based location methods, through totally summed difference between observed and theoretical arrival times is
usually adopted to build the objective function for source location. Since P-wave propagates fastest in seismic signal phases, the direct
P-wave arrival time has been widely used in locating seismic sources [6,15]. In contrast, S-wave usually has more energy and is less
affected by waveform attenuation, which has prompted researchers to locate seismic event using S-wave arrival time. Kuang et al. [16]
found that a common location result can be obtained from S-wave arrival times. The location result was enhanced after including the
correction incident angle. Gomberg et al. [17] and Engdahl et al. [18] carried out source location based on P- and S-wave arrival time
difference, while Zhou et al. [19] established a P–S phase arrival time difference and P-wave arrival time combined location method. In
addition, Zhou et al. [20] found that good location results can be obtained, by combining S-wave arrival time with one or multiple P-

The above introduction shows that it had better use P-wave arrival time for an AE event location strictly speaking. The observed P-
wave arrival time should be the summation of AE event occurrence time, travel time from source location to sensor location and PATSE
from sensor to signal storage where the PATSEs can be different between sensors. Furthermore, a multi-scale grid search strategy wil
be combined with the VFOM method [26] to thoroughly locate an AE event. A global view of the content and adopted strategy of this
study is shown in Fig. 1. The main innovations and contributions of this study are as follows: A distinct PATSE was observed through

5 Discussions
5.1 Improvement of the PATSE inversion
In the most simplified case, a PATSE does not change with time was adopted in the study. However, the PATSE may change with the
testing time. If the PATSE was treated as a variable with the time and event locations were treated as unknown parameters in the
PATSE inversion, the inversion dimension would sharply increase (dimension curse). Even after treating the event locations as known
parameters, there are still more than 10 dimensions (eight PATSEs plus the number
of PLB events). The commonly used Newton
iteration method and quasi-Newton iteration method converge quickly. However, they are highly dependent on the initial value and
easily fall into a locally optimum solution, especially for high-dimensional inversions [37]. Therefore, researchers have begun to use
global search algorithms, such as genetic algorithm, simulated annealing, PSO and Bayesian inversion. These methods can jump out of
local optimum solutions. However, they usually use random searches with low efficiency to obtain an optimum solution. Currently,
grid search is considered the most stable global inversion method, but its search speed is quite slow. Wang et al. [13] proposed a multi
scale grid search (coarse and fine grids) for inversion, which reduced the computation cost to some extent. Furthermore, research has
combined coarse grid search with a genetic algorithm, simulated annealing and Bayesian inversion; the coarse grid search can provide
a good initial solution for these global inversion algorithms [41]. In actual experiments or observation data, there may be no PLB
events, then the 3D locations, occurrence time of AE events and PATSEs of AE signals are related parameters in the high-dimension
inversion. Then, advanced inversion methods (e.g., trans-dimensional Bayesian inversion [33] and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo [42])
can be used for these high-dimensional inversions.
5.2 Influencing factors on AE event location accuracy
For an AE experiment on a small rock sample, the most common difficulty is that the AE location results are not consistent with the
failure mode of the rock sample. The AE location accuracy is affected by multiple factors. First, the data transmission rate is limited by
the AE monitoring system. With a signal sampling frequency of 1 MHz (i.e., 1 µs) and P-wave velocity of 3.6 mm/µs, the accumulation
effects of multiple P-wave sampling time errors may lead to a relatively large location error. Therefore, a higher signal sampling
frequency is necessary for a small sample test. Then, P-wave arrivals usually have small energy and the noise and propagation
attenuation can make the P-wave arrival unclear [10], which can lead to accumulation of errors. Our results showed that the average
PATSE (excluding sensor 8) reached 1.47 µs when the sensor 3 was taken as the reference, which is enough to complicate the AE event
location results in a small-size rock sample.
Meanwhile, the source location result is closely related to the objective location function. For example, the VFOM method is more
stable than the DL1 and DL2 methods (Fig. 4). Notably, the P-wave velocities in the rock compression process are different at various
times and locations. Owing to the stress differences and rock fractures, the velocity difference can reach 2,000 m/s [43,44]. In this
study, a homogeneous velocity model is adopted to reduce the location accuracy. In a future study, AE tomography can be applied to
obtain a real-time heterogeneous distributed 3D velocity model for the rock sample, then 3D velocity model-based location (e.g., 3D
ray shooting method [13]) can provide better location results.
6 Conclusions
To address the inferior location accuracy of AE events in a small sample, a Bayesian framework was established to invert the
PATSEs of AE signals and a multi-scale grid search algorithm was proposed for the VFOM location. The main conclusions are as follows:
(1) The existence of PATSE was found through PLB events and calculated using the proposed Bayesian inversion. (2) The average
location error of 25 PLB events was 14.30 mm and 6.58 mm, for PATSEs unremoved and removed data, respectively. This has shown
the necessity of removing PATSEs. (3) The combination of multi-scale grid search and VFOM location method was applied to an AE
event location, which had a better noise resistance to large P-wave arrival time picking errors than the DL1 and DL2 methods. (4) The
AE event location results with PATSE removed were in good correlation with the failure mode of the rock sample, which provides a
good approach for analysing the failure process of a small sample. Furthermore, improving the signal sampling frequency, developing
efficient global inversion algorithms and using a high-resolution 3D velocity model can improve the AE event location accuracy.
